title: ～た
summary: た on the end of a verb puts it in the past, the way friends say it: 来る (come), 来た (came).
parts: Verbs change their endings to say when, and whether, something happens. The plain past ends in た, or だ after some verbs.
This plain form is what you use with friends. The polite past, ～ました, comes later.

title: だ / です
summary: だ ends a sentence that says what something is: 成田だ, it's Narita. Friends say だ or leave it off; strangers and staff say です.
parts: だ comes at the very end of the sentence. In casual talk it's often left off, especially in questions.
です means the same thing, politely. You'll hear it from staff and strangers.

title: は
summary: は marks what you're talking about. It's written は but said "wa". On its own with a rising voice, it asks "what about…?"
parts: Where's the station? (What about the station?)
The topic comes first, then は, then what you say about it.

title: が
summary: が points at who or what does something, or what a description is about: 人が多い, there are lots of people.
parts: There are a lot of people.
は sets the topic for what follows; が picks out the one thing the sentence is about. Often either works, with a slightly different feel.

title: ～ない
summary: ない on a verb makes it negative, the way friends say it: わかる (understand), わからない (don't understand).
parts: The verb's ending changes before ない. For る verbs, drop る: 食べる, 食べない. For others, the last sound moves to the "a" row: わかる, わからない.

title: よ / ね / な / でしょ
summary: よ at the end tells someone something they don't know yet. ね looks for agreement, like "right?" or "huh". な is said half to yourself. でしょ? is surer: "told you".
parts: よ is friendly emphasis: you're filling the listener in.
ね assumes the listener sees it the same way.
な is ね said to yourself: a thought out loud, not a question for anyone.
でしょ? expects a yes: you knew it, and you're checking they see it too. Said flat, でしょう is a polite guess, "probably".

title: の
summary: の joins two nouns, like 's or "of": アレックスの部屋, Alex's room.
parts: The first noun owns or describes the second.

title: ～たい
summary: たい on a verb's stem means you want to do it: 食べる, 食べたい, want to eat.
parts: Drop る from a る verb, or move other verbs to their "i" sound, and add たい: やる, やりたい.
It changes like an adjective: 食べたくない is "don't want to eat".

title: を
summary: を marks what a verb is done to: ラーメンを食べる, eat ramen. It's said "o".
parts: Friends often drop it: ラーメン、食べる？ means the same.

title: も
summary: も means "too" or "also", in place of は, が or を: これも, this too.

title: です / ます
summary: Staff, strangers and bosses speak politely: verbs end in ます, and "is" is です. You'll hear it long before you need to say it.
parts: ます goes on a verb's stem, the same stem as たい: 食べます, 飲みます. Its negative is ません, and its past is ました.
Friends would say the plain form instead. Using ます with friends sounds distant; leaving it off with strangers sounds rude.
今日から、お願いします。

title: ～て / ～てください
summary: A verb's て form plus ください politely asks someone to do something. Friends just use the て form, which also links actions: do this, and then that.
parts: ちょっと待ってください！
The て form of 待つ is 待って. With friends, 待って on its own is enough.
ラーメンを食べて、ビールを飲む。
I eat ramen and drink a beer.
In the middle of a sentence, the て form means "and then": one action, then the next.

title: に
summary: に marks where something goes, or where it is: 店に来た, came to the shop.
parts: I came to the manga shop.
It also marks times: 朝に, in the morning. In casual talk it's sometimes dropped after places.

title: ～てる / ～ている
summary: A verb's て form plus いる says something is going on now. Friends shorten ている to てる.
parts: It can also mean a state that's ongoing: 知ってる, I know (I'm in the state of having learned it).

title: か
summary: か at the end of a polite sentence makes it a question: 好きです, I like it; 好きですか, do you like it?
parts: With friends, a rising voice is enough: 好き？ か on a plain sentence can sound blunt, so it mostly goes with です and ます.

title: で
summary: で marks where something happens: 公園で食べた, ate in the park. に is where something is or goes; で is where it's done.
parts: 公園でラーメンを食べた。
I ate ramen in the park.
で also marks what you use to do something, but that comes later.

title: から
summary: から after a reason means "because", and what follows is what happens: 寒いから, because it's cold.
parts: 寒いから、ラーメンがうまい。
It's cold, so ramen tastes great.
It's the same から as "from": the reason is where the rest comes from. It can end a sentence too: ベースだから。, because I play bass.

title: と
summary: と joins nouns, "A and B", or marks who you do something with: 店長と, with the manager.
parts: 店長とラーメンを食べた。
I ate ramen with the manager.
It joins whole lists, unlike や, which only gives examples. For "together", 一緒に often comes after it.

title: から / まで
summary: から marks where or when something starts; まで, where or when it ends: 朝まで, until morning.
parts: They work with places and times, together or apart.
